Media & American Studies
MC 2020 - New Media
Credits: 4
This introductory course explores new and emerging media through the lenses of history, technology, culture, and art.
Students will engage with theory and analysis, alongside hands-on creative exercises using mobile media technology.
Through readings, discussions, case studies, and experiments, we will examine new media aesthetics, storytelling
strategies, and tools like virtual and augmented reality, video games, and apps. This course also delves into the impact
of emerging media on journalism, documentary, activism, and its social and political implications.
When Offered:
Every year.
MC 2652 - Media Studies
Credits: 4
How can we comprehend and critique the media that immerse us? Let’s examine the media in the context of the political
and social economies within which they were developed. Drawing on a broad range of cultural theories, this course
addresses the functioning of media in a diverse and globalizing environment. A range of media is studied through
scholarship and primary texts: art, movies, advertisements, interviews, novels, short stories, and photographs.
(Formerly AS2652).
Prerequisites
EC I

MC 2802 - Multimedia Storytelling
Credits: 4
This hands-on course introduces students to nonfiction storytelling through text, photography, audio, video, and
immersive media. Students learn to observe closely, engage with people and places, and communicate clearly to specific
audiences-often through campus-based reporting. Through short projects such as photo stories, audio pieces, 360 video,
and micro-profiles, students practice visual communication, interviewing, and narrative structure. Emphasizing creative
expression, documentation, and peer critique, the course prepares students to craft compelling multimedia stories for
contemporary platforms. (Formerly AS2802).
When Offered:
Every semester.
MC 2901 - Introduction to Video & TV
Credits: 4
In this introductory course, students will learn the basics of television and video production: camera operation, sound,
lighting and editing for field and studio production. Through hands-on workshops, screenings, lectures and readings,
students will explore the visual language of the moving image as well as the conventional and experimental approaches
to non-fiction video, students will learn to use moving images and sound for artistic expression and as a tool for
effective communication. Students will complete individual video projects shot in the field as well as a collaborative TV
broadcast project produced in the television studio. (Formerly AS3247).
When Offered:
Every Semester
MC 2902 - Introduction to Radio Production
Credits: 4
Learn the basic techniques of radio production. Students will learn basic interviewing skills, studio production and
mixing techniques, and how to manipulate digital audio recordings in post-production using industry editing software.

MC 2910 - Podcasting and Audio Storytelling
Credits: 4
This media production course explores audio podcasting in many forms and includes lessons on recording,
interviewing, script writing, narration, editing and sound mixing. The class will focus on developing engaging content
and creative techniques for non-fiction storytelling through sound. Students will be encouraged to develop stories from
their unique point-of-view, embedded in their communities or building on their academic research. We will explore
voice in a number of ways: technical (on-air reporting voice), creative (directorial voice), and socio-political (amplifying
historically underrepresented voices). Each week we will review professional podcasts which will serve as mentor texts
for students as they produce their own projects. Student work will be reviewed at various stages of production, with
regular peer and instructor critiques, allowing for an iterative creative process of output, feedback and revision.
(Formerly AS3010).
Prerequisites
EC-I
When Offered:

MC 3622 - Sports, Media, and Society
Credits: 4
Explore the prominent place of sports in the United States and other societies, and how media narratives about sports
and athletes shape individual, group, and national identities. What is the relationship of sports to larger questions of
identity, politics, economics, and history? The course illuminates how class, race, gender, sexuality, and nation interplay
in our understanding of sports, media, society, and culture. (Formerly AS3622).
Prerequisites

Credits: 4
A history of film in the United States from the 1890’s to the present. It examines the social, political, economic, and
cultural changes of different eras in relation to the emergence and popularization of modern cinema. Students must see
and comment on all the films shown in the course. (Formerly AS3632).

collaborative works and applied practices. Students will complete individual and group projects and presentations.
(Formerly AS3700).

Western, the melodrama, the gangster film, science fiction, horror, and musical comedy. The course investigates the
connection between genre forms and the development of Hollywood mythology and U.S. ideology. (Formerly AS3712).

EC II

MC 3722 - History of Mass Media
Credits: 4
Learn the history of the mass media. We will examine the parts played by government, private enterprise, social
movements, and technology in the development of the media. In addition to the political economy of the media, the
course will cover the conflicts over civil liberties, mass culture, advertising, and the rise of consumer culture in America.
(Formerly AS3722).
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Every year.
MC 3732 - Politics of Media
Credits: 4
Using a broad definition of politics - not only the world of elections or of governance, but of power relations in everyday
life - this course examines how political structures affect the mass media, and how the mass media are a strong influence
in politics. The ways in which the media promotes democracy and citizenship, but also constricts democracy, are central
to the course. The branding of culture, corporate consolidation, and the images of women and minorities in the media
are all examined, as are various forms of the media including film, the Internet, and television. (Formerly AS3732).
Prerequisites

MC 3735 - Documentary Media Studies
Credits: 4
What is reality? Can truth be captured and represented? Learn about documentary film, photography and new media
projects from the birth of photography to today. Watch and critique seminal documentary projects. Explore documentary
as political expression, entertainment, art, journalism, propaganda and self-portrait. Lectures, readings and discussions
focus on forms and styles of non-fiction storytelling, the role of documentaries in society, and documentary ethics and
practice. (Formerly AS3735).

United States, Europe, Latin America and Africa. It explores film form as well as content and their relationship to each
other. (Formerly AS3742).

Credits: 4
This course examines the social, historical, and technological construction of film as a medium as well as the social and
technological construction of gender. By looking at contemporary American films, students will reflect upon and critique
the various representations of gender conformity and fluidity. The intent of the class is to both expand an understanding
of gender and to identify the ways in which film reinforces binary notions of gender and gender roles. (Formerly
AS3745).
Prerequisites
EC II
MC 3750 - AI & Society
Credits: 4
Artificial Intelligence technologies are being integrated into our lives. What do you need to know about Artificial
Intelligence? Will it disrupt everything? Will you survive? Could you even thrive in the wake of this A.I. tsunami? A.I. &
Society begins with the fundamentals of A.I. literacy by explaining foundational concepts. Understanding these
fundamentals, we will develop a complex analysis of the positive and negative effects of this technological revolution.
What predictions can we make for our A.I. future? What are the dangers of an accelerated adoption of untested
technologies? Can A.I. be aligned with human values? Will we prosper as augmented humans empowered by artificial
general intelligence? How will A.I. impact our personal, professional and political lives? (Formerly AS3750).
Prerequisites
ECII
When Offered:
Every year.

Credits: 4
A history of American popular music: Follow changes in American musical culture from work songs and parlor pianos
to auto-tune and streaming media. This course will cover the cultures, politics, and economics of music-making and
profit-taking in the history of popular music, the music business, and the media in the U.S. (Formerly AS3810).

MC 3822 - TV and Radio Journalism
Credits: 4
This course explores the history, the present situation and possible future of electronic journalism in the United States. It
is also a practical course in which students work toward proficiency in television and radio journalism. They learn about
– and do – newswriting, newscasting and, utilizing the College’s television studio, join together in producing television
programs. They also work on field reporting or electronic news gathering. There is training in the use of audio
equipment, cameras and a special effects generator or switcher. The basics of editing using the College’s television
editing laboratory are explored. Students write papers which critique and compare news programs on television.
(Formerly AS3822).

newspapers, magazines, books, radio, records, movies, and television. The course will explore the viewpoints of

MC 4700 - Digital PR Campaigns
Credits: 4
This hands-on course explores the strategies and tools used in public relations and digital media making. Students will
work in teams to develop and execute PR campaigns for various organizations, incorporating social media, content
marketing, outreach, and analytics. Through case studies, industry insights, and applications, students will learn how to
create effective digital narratives, manage online reputations, and assess campaign effectiveness. By the end of the
course, students will have designed a comprehensive digital PR campaign, gaining valuable experience in strategic
communication and collaboration. (Formerly AS4700).

MC 4722 - Film: Ideas and Aesthetics
Credits: 4
The course treats film in relation to modern theories and aesthetic techniques and offers tools for developing an in-depth
analysis of film form and content. Instructor may focus upon the ideas and aesthetics of particular chronological eras,
auteurs, and film movements such as African American cinema or feminist filmmaking. The primary focus is to
introduce the complexity of film analysis within the framework of close readings of specific films. (Formerly AS4722).
Prerequisites

MC 4729 - Media & Popular Culture
Credits: 4
This course focuses on the relationship between media genres and different forms of popular culture. Students explore
different theoretical approaches to the understanding the role of media in modern society. The course examines how
popular media communicate ideas about the world, about identity, and our sense of self. Reading across social media,
gaming, television, film, music, art, and the popular press, the course considers relationships between the media,
institutions, identity, relations of power, and historical, economic, social, and political contexts. (Formerly AS4729).

MC 4732 - Political Film
Credits: 4
From wars and elections, to civil rights and civil liberties, feature films and documentaries have influenced American
public opinion and policies. Through in-class screenings and discussion, this course will examine the historical period in
which selected motion pictures were produced and explore the immediate and long-term impact of the films. The
screenings may include Do the Right Thing, Fahrenheit 9/11, and Easy Rider. (Formerly AS4732).
Prerequisites
EMS and one of the following: AS2112 or AS2122 or AS2252 or AS2262 or AS2263 or AS2300 or AS2640 or AS3215 or
AS3222 or AS3270 or AS3462; Or permission of instructor
When Offered:
Occasionally.
MC 4735 - Latin American Cultures & Media
Credits: 4
In this course, we explore the histories and cultures of Latin American heritage communities in the U.S. with a focus on
media. Using an interdisciplinary approach, we will examine how media shapes culture, identity, and social and
economic power dynamics. Through readings, lectures, screenings, listening exercises, and class discussions, we will
reflect on how these communities have been portrayed and have portrayed themselves across media over time. We will
focus on the historical and political factors that influence media industries, narrative production, the formation of
stereotypes, and how creators have challenged those stereotypes. While covering media such as the printed press, radio,
television, and digital platforms, our main focus will be on cinema. We will analyze how class, gender, ethnicity, race,
and citizenship are represented and shaped both individual identities and collective stories. We will also explore how
migration and immigration and activism have shaped people’s experiences and media practices as well as the
connections that remain and emerge with communities across borders. (Formerly AS4735).
Prerequisites
EMS and AS 2112 or AS 2122 or AS 2252 or AS 2263 or AS 2300 or AS 2640 or AS 3215 or AS 3222 or AS 3270 or AS 3462

11/7/26, 2:12 PM Course Descriptions - SUNY Old Westbury
Credits: 4
What is now called investigative Reporting is an especially American journalistic pursuit of exposing corruption and
abuses by individuals and institutions, inequity and unfairness, and revealing danger. The theory of this journalistic
form is that if people are informed of such problems, they will demand a resolution. The course focuses on the
philosophy and history of the enterprise, from the crusading journalism of the early years of the press in what became
the United States, through the Muckraking Era of the early 20th century, through Watergate, through the founding of
Investigative Reporters and Editors, to the present investigative reporting scene in print, radio, television and on the
Internet. Students will conduct research on the history of investigative reporting. They will learn techniques of
investigation and proof and do their own investigative reporting in print or electronic forms of media. (Formerly
AS4802).
Prerequisites
EMS
When Offered:
Every year.

MC 4850 - Digital Revolution
Credits: 4
We are in the midst of a profound technological and historical change: the Digital Revolution. Digital networks of
communication permeate nearly every aspect of our life, yet we understand very little about them, their historical
development, conflicts over their use, and their impact on our way of life. This course will look at the cultural,
technological, economic, and political impact of the digital revolution. (Formerly AS4850).

Credits: 4

fiction video production. Through readings, class descriptions, screenings of existing documentaries and student work-
in progress, students develop their own voices as media makers, moving beyond traditional structures and notions of
“objectivity” to explore documentary as artistic social expression. (Formerly AS4852).

MC 5200 - Environmental Journalism
Credits: 4
Environmental journalism has roots extending back to the writings of early American naturalists and conservationists. It
began taking its contemporary form with the publication in 1962 of the book Silent Spring by Rachel Carson which
called wide public attention to the impacts of pesticides. The class considers the writings of early naturalists and moves
on to the work and legacy of Rachel Carson and the emergence of environmental journalism as a distinct area of
journalism practiced in all media. Students write articles and some produce audio and video pieces on environmental
issues. The course provides Media & Communications majors with a widening of their perspective, and for those
majoring in biology, chemistry and physics a furthering of their skills at communication. Also, it is geared for those
focused on politics, government, law and other public policy fields because of the great impact of environmental issues
on them. It is a component of the college’s Environmental Studies minor. (Formerly AS5200). 
Prerequisites
One of the following: AS2112 or AS2122 or AS2252 or AS2262 or AS2263 or AS2300 or AS2640 or AS3215 or AS3222 or
AS3270 or AS3462
AND EMS
Or permission of instructor

Credits: 4

Can American democracy survive in a society dominated by powerful media and sophisticated mass persuasion? This
senior seminar is a history of war and political propaganda with a focus on the role of propaganda in the conflicts
between social movements and powerful institutions. The rise of public relations and its role in politics and the mass
media will be an important theme. (Formerly AS5420).
Prerequisites
One of the following: AS2112 or AS2122 or AS2252 or AS2262 or AS2263 or AS2300 or AS2640 or AS3215 or AS3222 or
AS3270 or AS3462
AND EMS
Or permission of instructor
When Offered:
Every year.
MC 5720 - Senior Media Project
Credits: 4
This capstone seminar is designed for advanced students to develop an independent project under the mentorship of
faculty while participating in an advanced media production course. The final project must align with the course’s focus
on medium, craft, and structure. Students are required to meet with the professor before the semester begins to develop
and obtain approval for a detailed project plan and timeline. Throughout the semester, students must attend all classes,
provide peer support, and demonstrate production best practices. They are responsible for completing all course
assignments and meeting deadlines unless modifications are approved by the professor to accommodate their capstone
project. In addition to the capstone project, students are expected to create a comprehensive proposal and timeline, meet
regularly with the professor for feedback and support outside of class, and maintain a weekly process reflection journal.
(Formerly AS5720).
Prerequisites
Permission of Instructor.
When Offered:
Every Semester

MC 5725 - Senior Media Portfolio

as a blended course with a mix of online and face-to-face instruction. (Formerly AS5725).

MC 5862 - The Journalist as Creative Writer
Credits: 4
Many American journalists have written fiction and creative nonfiction. This course examines both types of writing and
studies, for example, the works of Mark Twain, Ernest Hemingway, Joan Didion, Alex Haley, and Hunter Thompson. It
explores “personal journalism” and the “new journalism” of the sixties and seventies. Students will practice literary
journalism themselves by writing several fiction and non-fiction pieces. (Formerly AS5862).
Prerequisites
One of the following: AS2112 or AS2122 or AS2252 or AS2262 or AS2263 or AS2300 or AS2640 or AS3215 or AS3222 or
AS3270 or AS3462

records.title: New Media
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This introductory course explores new and emerging media through the lenses of history, technology, culture, and art.
Students will engage with theory and analysis, alongside hands-on creative exercises using mobile media technology.
Through readings, discussions, case studies, and experiments, we will examine new media aesthetics, storytelling
strategies, and tools like virtual and augmented reality, video games, and apps. This course also delves into the impact
of emerging media on journalism, documentary, activism, and its social and political implications.
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Media Studies
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
How can we comprehend and critique the media that immerse us? Let’s examine the media in the context of the political
and social economies within which they were developed. Drawing on a broad range of cultural theories, this course
addresses the functioning of media in a diverse and globalizing environment. A range of media is studied through
scholarship and primary texts: art, movies, advertisements, interviews, novels, short stories, and photographs.
(Formerly AS2652).
Prerequisites
EC I

When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: Multimedia Storytelling
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This hands-on course introduces students to nonfiction storytelling through text, photography, audio, video, and
immersive media. Students learn to observe closely, engage with people and places, and communicate clearly to specific
audiences-often through campus-based reporting. Through short projects such as photo stories, audio pieces, 360 video,
and micro-profiles, students practice visual communication, interviewing, and narrative structure. Emphasizing creative
expression, documentation, and peer critique, the course prepares students to craft compelling multimedia stories for
contemporary platforms. (Formerly AS2802).
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Introduction to Video & TV
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
In this introductory course, students will learn the basics of television and video production: camera operation, sound,
lighting and editing for field and studio production. Through hands-on workshops, screenings, lectures and readings,
students will explore the visual language of the moving image as well as the conventional and experimental approaches
to non-fiction video, students will learn to use moving images and sound for artistic expression and as a tool for
effective communication. Students will complete individual video projects shot in the field as well as a collaborative TV
broadcast project produced in the television studio. (Formerly AS3247).
When Offered:
Every Semester

records.title: Introduction to Radio Production
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Learn the basic techniques of radio production. Students will learn basic interviewing skills, studio production and
mixing techniques, and how to manipulate digital audio recordings in post-production using industry editing software.

Learn the basics of the three phases of production, including how to plan, script, create and edit radio content at the
college radio station, OWWR, Old Westbury Web Radio. (Formerly AS3820).
When Offered:
Every Semester

records.title: Podcasting and Audio Storytelling
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This media production course explores audio podcasting in many forms and includes lessons on recording,
interviewing, script writing, narration, editing and sound mixing. The class will focus on developing engaging content
and creative techniques for non-fiction storytelling through sound. Students will be encouraged to develop stories from
their unique point-of-view, embedded in their communities or building on their academic research. We will explore
voice in a number of ways: technical (on-air reporting voice), creative (directorial voice), and socio-political (amplifying
historically underrepresented voices). Each week we will review professional podcasts which will serve as mentor texts
for students as they produce their own projects. Student work will be reviewed at various stages of production, with
regular peer and instructor critiques, allowing for an iterative creative process of output, feedback and revision.
(Formerly AS3010).
Prerequisites
EC-I
When Offered:
Other

records.title: Sports, Media, and Society
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Explore the prominent place of sports in the United States and other societies, and how media narratives about sports
and athletes shape individual, group, and national identities. What is the relationship of sports to larger questions of
identity, politics, economics, and history? The course illuminates how class, race, gender, sexuality, and nation interplay
in our understanding of sports, media, society, and culture. (Formerly AS3622).
Prerequisites

EC II

records.title: History of U.S. Film
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
A history of film in the United States from the 1890’s to the present. It examines the social, political, economic, and
cultural changes of different eras in relation to the emergence and popularization of modern cinema. Students must see
and comment on all the films shown in the course. (Formerly AS3632).
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: PR & Strategic Communications
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course examines the role of strategic communication and its applications in today’s world. In this intermediate
course students will gain knowledge and skills about the role of strategic communications through case studies,
collaborative works and applied practices. Students will complete individual and group projects and presentations.
(Formerly AS3700).
Prerequisites
ECII
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: American Film Genres
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

An in-depth examination of classic genres of films in the United States. Genres studied may include silent comedy, the
Western, the melodrama, the gangster film, science fiction, horror, and musical comedy. The course investigates the
connection between genre forms and the development of Hollywood mythology and U.S. ideology. (Formerly AS3712).
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: History of Mass Media
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Learn the history of the mass media. We will examine the parts played by government, private enterprise, social
movements, and technology in the development of the media. In addition to the political economy of the media, the
course will cover the conflicts over civil liberties, mass culture, advertising, and the rise of consumer culture in America.
(Formerly AS3722).
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Politics of Media
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Using a broad definition of politics - not only the world of elections or of governance, but of power relations in everyday
life - this course examines how political structures affect the mass media, and how the mass media are a strong influence
in politics. The ways in which the media promotes democracy and citizenship, but also constricts democracy, are central
to the course. The branding of culture, corporate consolidation, and the images of women and minorities in the media
are all examined, as are various forms of the media including film, the Internet, and television. (Formerly AS3732).
Prerequisites

EC II
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Documentary Media Studies
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
What is reality? Can truth be captured and represented? Learn about documentary film, photography and new media
projects from the birth of photography to today. Watch and critique seminal documentary projects. Explore documentary
as political expression, entertainment, art, journalism, propaganda and self-portrait. Lectures, readings and discussions
focus on forms and styles of non-fiction storytelling, the role of documentaries in society, and documentary ethics and
practice. (Formerly AS3735).
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: Myths and Images in Film
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course examines the movies in terms of social myths and social values. It looks at representative films from the
United States, Europe, Latin America and Africa. It explores film form as well as content and their relationship to each
other. (Formerly AS3742).
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: Film and Gender
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course examines the social, historical, and technological construction of film as a medium as well as the social and
technological construction of gender. By looking at contemporary American films, students will reflect upon and critique
the various representations of gender conformity and fluidity. The intent of the class is to both expand an understanding
of gender and to identify the ways in which film reinforces binary notions of gender and gender roles. (Formerly
AS3745).
Prerequisites
EC II

records.title: AI & Society
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Artificial Intelligence technologies are being integrated into our lives. What do you need to know about Artificial
Intelligence? Will it disrupt everything? Will you survive? Could you even thrive in the wake of this A.I. tsunami? A.I. &
Society begins with the fundamentals of A.I. literacy by explaining foundational concepts. Understanding these
fundamentals, we will develop a complex analysis of the positive and negative effects of this technological revolution.
What predictions can we make for our A.I. future? What are the dangers of an accelerated adoption of untested
technologies? Can A.I. be aligned with human values? Will we prosper as augmented humans empowered by artificial
general intelligence? How will A.I. impact our personal, professional and political lives? (Formerly AS3750).
Prerequisites
ECII
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Writing for Media
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The course combines instruction in the craft of journalism and teaches students to write accurately and clearly and to
meet deadlines. The basics of good reporting whether for print, broadcast, or internet journalism are stressed, including
how to gather and verify information, where to look for stories, how to interview, how to use sources, and how to report

in a fair and balanced manner. Students will write about and cover a variety of news events and issues. (Formerly
AS3800).
Prerequisites
EMS
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Music and Media
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
A history of American popular music: Follow changes in American musical culture from work songs and parlor pianos
to auto-tune and streaming media. This course will cover the cultures, politics, and economics of music-making and
profit-taking in the history of popular music, the music business, and the media in the U.S. (Formerly AS3810).
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: TV and Radio Journalism
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course explores the history, the present situation and possible future of electronic journalism in the United States. It
is also a practical course in which students work toward proficiency in television and radio journalism. They learn about
– and do – newswriting, newscasting and, utilizing the College’s television studio, join together in producing television
programs. They also work on field reporting or electronic news gathering. There is training in the use of audio
equipment, cameras and a special effects generator or switcher. The basics of editing using the College’s television
editing laboratory are explored. Students write papers which critique and compare news programs on television.
(Formerly AS3822).
Prerequisites

EC II
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: Public Relations and Society
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The course examines the role of public relations in the media, corporate culture, politics and society. This is an
intermediate-level course that is designed for students who previously have not taken formal instruction in public
relations. Students receive instruction in the basics of public relations and perform exercises intended to equip them
with a working knowledge of the field. (Formerly AS3830).
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Multimedia Newsroom
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This fast-paced, intermediate course provides students practical experience in multimedia reporting across a variety of
topics. Emphasizing accuracy, clarity, and ethical standards, the course guides students from the pitch process through
researching, interviewing, writing and editing. Students will develop professional reporting skills and an understanding
of journalistic responsibility in serving an informed and engaged audience. (Formerly AS3835).
Prerequisites
AS2802 or MC2802 AND AS3800 or MC2802
AND EMS
OR permission of instructor

When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: African Americans and the Mass Media
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Examines the participation of African‑Americans in the development of mass media in the U.S. by looking at
newspapers, magazines, books, radio, records, movies, and television. The course will explore the viewpoints of
African‑Americans through the mass media, how they are presented and represented, and how the white-owned media
influences African-American images. (Formerly AS3842).
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: Women and the Media
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course explores the ways women are depicted by the mass media and how that depiction has changed over time. It
also investigates the role of women in the media professions. (Formerly AS3852).
Prerequisites
EC II

records.title: Special Topics in Media Production
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course addresses a special topic in media production. The specific topic will be announced by the Department
when offered. The course may be taken for credit up to three times if the course topic changes. (Formerly AS3860).

Prerequisites
MC 2802 or AS2802
AND ECII
Or instructor permission.
When Offered:
Occasionally

records.title: Radio on the Air
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Acquire advanced production techniques and radio programming skills. Learn advanced interviewing skills, production
and mixing techniques, and advance your digital audio recording and editing skills. Gain proficiency with
programming, and monitor issues and trends in the industry. Students will produce a live weekly news and
entertainment magazine radio show on the college radio station, OWWR, Old Westbury Web Radio. (Formerly AS4150).
Prerequisites
MC2902 or AS2902 or AS3820
ECII
Or permission of instructor.
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Special Topics in Media Studies
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Offers an in-depth exploration of a special topic in media studies, in an area defined by the instructor. Topics might
include political campaigns and the media; the first amendment; public and private spheres in the digital age;
“branding”; or a specific musical or film genre (such as a course in Rock and Roll, the Blues, or the Hollywood Musical).

The course allows for a deeper theoretical, historical, institutional and/or political analysis of media and its power in
American life. Students can take more than once as an Independent Study. (Formerly AS4160).
Prerequisites
EMS
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: New Media Beat
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Students will be immersed in an intensive, fast-paced environment that reflects real world experience in the media
industry. Emphasis will be placed on writing, critical thinking, and creativity. The course will also explore the technical,
philosophical, and practical elements of online journalism. By the end of this course students will have acquired a
multitude of skills that will give them a competitive edge in the media field. (Formerly AS4260).
Prerequisites
MC2802 or AS2802
AND EMS
Or permission of instructor.
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Global Media
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The American media compete in a global market. American media have become a dominant source of information and
entertainment world wide. The course will examine the role of the American corporate media in a world of increasing
global political, economic, and cultural competition, and collaboration. It will also examine the rise of new media
alternatives in reaction to the dominance of the global corporate media. (Formerly AS4280).

Prerequisites
EMS
Or permission of instructor.
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: Feature Writing
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This is a practical course in the basics of writing feature articles for newspapers and magazines. Students learn how to
research, write, and edit feature articles. They will study the different techniques used in a variety of feature articles -
human interest, travel, seasonal, humor, sports, science, personality profiles, and personal experiences - and write such
articles themselves. (Formerly AS4442).
Prerequisites
AS3800 or MC3800
Or permission of instructor
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Digital PR Campaigns
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This hands-on course explores the strategies and tools used in public relations and digital media making. Students will
work in teams to develop and execute PR campaigns for various organizations, incorporating social media, content
marketing, outreach, and analytics. Through case studies, industry insights, and applications, students will learn how to
create effective digital narratives, manage online reputations, and assess campaign effectiveness. By the end of the
course, students will have designed a comprehensive digital PR campaign, gaining valuable experience in strategic
communication and collaboration. (Formerly AS4700).

Prerequisites
MC2802 or AS2802; MC3700 or AS3700
Or permission of instructor.
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Film: Ideas and Aesthetics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The course treats film in relation to modern theories and aesthetic techniques and offers tools for developing an in-depth
analysis of film form and content. Instructor may focus upon the ideas and aesthetics of particular chronological eras,
auteurs, and film movements such as African American cinema or feminist filmmaking. The primary focus is to
introduce the complexity of film analysis within the framework of close readings of specific films. (Formerly AS4722).
Prerequisites
EMS
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: Media & Popular Culture
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course focuses on the relationship between media genres and different forms of popular culture. Students explore
different theoretical approaches to the understanding the role of media in modern society. The course examines how
popular media communicate ideas about the world, about identity, and our sense of self. Reading across social media,
gaming, television, film, music, art, and the popular press, the course considers relationships between the media,
institutions, identity, relations of power, and historical, economic, social, and political contexts. (Formerly AS4729).
Prerequisites
EMS and AS 2122 or AS 2251 or AS 2226 or AS 2263 or AS 2300 or AS 2640 or AS 3215 or AS 3222 or AS 3270 or AS 3462

records.title: Political Film
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
From wars and elections, to civil rights and civil liberties, feature films and documentaries have influenced American
public opinion and policies. Through in-class screenings and discussion, this course will examine the historical period in
which selected motion pictures were produced and explore the immediate and long-term impact of the films. The
screenings may include Do the Right Thing, Fahrenheit 9/11, and Easy Rider. (Formerly AS4732).
Prerequisites
EMS and one of the following: AS2112 or AS2122 or AS2252 or AS2262 or AS2263 or AS2300 or AS2640 or AS3215 or
AS3222 or AS3270 or AS3462; Or permission of instructor
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: Latin American Cultures & Media
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
In this course, we explore the histories and cultures of Latin American heritage communities in the U.S. with a focus on
media. Using an interdisciplinary approach, we will examine how media shapes culture, identity, and social and
economic power dynamics. Through readings, lectures, screenings, listening exercises, and class discussions, we will
reflect on how these communities have been portrayed and have portrayed themselves across media over time. We will
focus on the historical and political factors that influence media industries, narrative production, the formation of
stereotypes, and how creators have challenged those stereotypes. While covering media such as the printed press, radio,
television, and digital platforms, our main focus will be on cinema. We will analyze how class, gender, ethnicity, race,
and citizenship are represented and shaped both individual identities and collective stories. We will also explore how
migration and immigration and activism have shaped people’s experiences and media practices as well as the
connections that remain and emerge with communities across borders. (Formerly AS4735).
Prerequisites
EMS and AS 2112 or AS 2122 or AS 2252 or AS 2263 or AS 2300 or AS 2640 or AS 3215 or AS 3222 or AS 3270 or AS 3462

records.title: Investigative Reporting
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
What is now called investigative Reporting is an especially American journalistic pursuit of exposing corruption and
abuses by individuals and institutions, inequity and unfairness, and revealing danger. The theory of this journalistic
form is that if people are informed of such problems, they will demand a resolution. The course focuses on the
philosophy and history of the enterprise, from the crusading journalism of the early years of the press in what became
the United States, through the Muckraking Era of the early 20th century, through Watergate, through the founding of
Investigative Reporters and Editors, to the present investigative reporting scene in print, radio, television and on the
Internet. Students will conduct research on the history of investigative reporting. They will learn techniques of
investigation and proof and do their own investigative reporting in print or electronic forms of media. (Formerly
AS4802).
Prerequisites
EMS
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Editing For Publication
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This is an advanced journalism course in which students receive intense preparation in reporting and writing for
newspapers, magazines and the internet. (Formerly AS4812).
Prerequisites
MC2802 or AS2802; MC3800 or AS3800
AND EMS
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: Digital News Lab
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

This advanced course immerses students in hands-on, collaborative production of the university’s multimedia digital
news site, The Catalyst. Students produce original content on deadline that meets professional standards and learn the
essential ethical, technical, and editorial practices that inform and engage a digital audience via the written word,
photography, audio, video and social media. (Formerly AS4822).
Prerequisites
MC2802 or AS2802
AND MC3800 or AS3800 or MC3835 or AS3835;
AND EMS
Or Permission of Instructor
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Internship in Journalism and Media
records.sourceText:
Credits: 1‑12
This internship provides students with hands-on experience working at a campus media outlet (OWWR, The Catalyst,
Media Innovation Center/OWTV) or in a professional media setting such as a news organization, production studio,
digital platform, or network. Students develop practical skills in a real-life environment and meet with the instructor to
discuss their progress and write about their experience. The internship is an excellent opportunity for students who are
interested in a media career to gain experience, expand their skill set, build their resume, and develop contacts. Select
internships also provide opportunities for portfolio development with instructor guidance. (Formerly AS4832).
Prerequisites
Permission of instructor
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Media Innovation Center Fellows
records.sourceText:
Credits: 1-12

Media Innovation Center (MIC) Fellows is an advanced, hands-on course for students who have demonstrated
competency in media production who are ready to develop their media portfolios further and contribute meaningfully
to the MIC. Students work independently on a self-directed media project(s) that supports the MIC and its mission.
(Formerly AS4835).
Prerequisites
Permission of Instructor.
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Digital Revolution
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
We are in the midst of a profound technological and historical change: the Digital Revolution. Digital networks of
communication permeate nearly every aspect of our life, yet we understand very little about them, their historical
development, conflicts over their use, and their impact on our way of life. This course will look at the cultural,
technological, economic, and political impact of the digital revolution. (Formerly AS4850).
Prerequisites
EMS.
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: Advanced Video: Documentary
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Produce, shoot and edit original documentary videos. Explore the fundamental techniques of and approaches to non-
fiction video production. Through readings, class descriptions, screenings of existing documentaries and student work-
in progress, students develop their own voices as media makers, moving beyond traditional structures and notions of
“objectivity” to explore documentary as artistic social expression. (Formerly AS4852).

Prerequisites
MC2802 or AS2802; MC2901 or AS2901 or AS3247
Or permission of instructor
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Advanced TV: Studio Production
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course advances students’ understanding and execution of television production. Students learn the three stages of
production: how to script, plan, and produce a segment; how to set up and shoot; and how to package it during the
editing process. (Formerly AS4870).
Prerequisites
MC2802 or AS2802; MC2901 or AS2901 or AS3247
Or permission of instructor.
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Radio Reporting
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Learn the ethics and practices of radio journalism. This course emphasizes news content and develops radio reporting
skills in the field and on-air. We will review the business of news and news gathering, working with acquiring sound
bites, actualities and natural sound, seasonal and specialized coverage, programming and management decisions,
criteria and types of stories, and the roles of social media and the internet. Students will be using digital field reporting
technologies to produce, and broadcast a live weekly news radio show on the college radio station, OWWR, Old
Westbury Web Radio. (Formerly AS4882).
Prerequisites
MC2802 or AS2802; MC3800 or AS3800

Course Descriptions - SUNY Old Westbury
When Offered:
Occasionally.

Sports, Talk, Public Affairs, or Entertainment programming as defined by the instructor. Students learn the value of
collaboration through hands-on experience. (Formerly AS4935).
Prerequisites
MC2901 or AS 3247; or MC4870 or AS3870
Or permission of instructor.

records.title: Environmental Journalism
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Environmental journalism has roots extending back to the writings of early American naturalists and conservationists. It
began taking its contemporary form with the publication in 1962 of the book Silent Spring by Rachel Carson which
called wide public attention to the impacts of pesticides. The class considers the writings of early naturalists and moves
on to the work and legacy of Rachel Carson and the emergence of environmental journalism as a distinct area of
journalism practiced in all media. Students write articles and some produce audio and video pieces on environmental
issues. The course provides Media & Communications majors with a widening of their perspective, and for those
majoring in biology, chemistry and physics a furthering of their skills at communication. Also, it is geared for those
focused on politics, government, law and other public policy fields because of the great impact of environmental issues
on them. It is a component of the college’s Environmental Studies minor. (Formerly AS5200). 
Prerequisites
One of the following: AS2112 or AS2122 or AS2252 or AS2262 or AS2263 or AS2300 or AS2640 or AS3215 or AS3222 or
AS3270 or AS3462
AND EMS
Or permission of instructor

records.title: Propaganda and Mass Persuasion
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

Can American democracy survive in a society dominated by powerful media and sophisticated mass persuasion? This
senior seminar is a history of war and political propaganda with a focus on the role of propaganda in the conflicts
between social movements and powerful institutions. The rise of public relations and its role in politics and the mass
media will be an important theme. (Formerly AS5420).
Prerequisites
One of the following: AS2112 or AS2122 or AS2252 or AS2262 or AS2263 or AS2300 or AS2640 or AS3215 or AS3222 or
AS3270 or AS3462
AND EMS
Or permission of instructor
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: Senior Media Project
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This capstone seminar is designed for advanced students to develop an independent project under the mentorship of
faculty while participating in an advanced media production course. The final project must align with the course’s focus
on medium, craft, and structure. Students are required to meet with the professor before the semester begins to develop
and obtain approval for a detailed project plan and timeline. Throughout the semester, students must attend all classes,
provide peer support, and demonstrate production best practices. They are responsible for completing all course
assignments and meeting deadlines unless modifications are approved by the professor to accommodate their capstone
project. In addition to the capstone project, students are expected to create a comprehensive proposal and timeline, meet
regularly with the professor for feedback and support outside of class, and maintain a weekly process reflection journal.
(Formerly AS5720).
Prerequisites
Permission of Instructor.
When Offered:
Every Semester

records.title: Senior Media Portfolio
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
In this capstone production course, students create an online media portfolio in their chosen medium. Throughout the
term, work samples are developed and improved through individualized study and regular critique. Typically offered
as a blended course with a mix of online and face-to-face instruction. (Formerly AS5725).
Prerequisites
Permission of instructor.
When Offered:
Every year.

records.title: The Journalist as Creative Writer
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Many American journalists have written fiction and creative nonfiction. This course examines both types of writing and
studies, for example, the works of Mark Twain, Ernest Hemingway, Joan Didion, Alex Haley, and Hunter Thompson. It
explores “personal journalism” and the “new journalism” of the sixties and seventies. Students will practice literary
journalism themselves by writing several fiction and non-fiction pieces. (Formerly AS5862).
Prerequisites
One of the following: AS2112 or AS2122 or AS2252 or AS2262 or AS2263 or AS2300 or AS2640 or AS3215 or AS3222 or
AS3270 or AS3462
AND EMS
Or permission of instructor
When Offered:
Every year.
